title: Erasure surface code circuit without mid-circuit erasure checks
authors: Margaret Pavlovich, Ivan Rojkov, Chen Wang, Shruti Puri
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) codes can correct twice as many erasure errors as Pauli errors. Because of this scaling advantage, there is significant interest in developing qubits whose dominant error channel can be converted into erasures via mid-circuit erasure checks. However, such erasure checks come with hardware overhead in practice. End-of-the-line three-state readout, in which one simultaneously measures a qubit's erasure status and computational state, is an alternative to mid-circuit erasure checks that is generally simpler to implement. In this work, we systematically study the conditions required to enable erasure performance---the doubled error-correction capacity---in the surface code with and without mid-circuit erasure checks. We introduce the moonwalking surface code, the time-reversal of the walking surface code, as a zero-overhead circuit with superior handling of leakage and erasure. Specifically, we show that it enables erasure-like logical error rate scaling when combined with three-state measurement if leaked qubits cause two-qubit gates to be skipped and an appropriate decoder is used. Our decoder, based on a branch-and-bound algorithm, specifically incorporates the noise structure of the skip-gate leaked-qubit effect.
summary: This paper advances quantum error correction theory by proposing the 'moonwalking surface code' as an efficient alternative to traditional circuits. It achieves superior erasure error correction capacity using only simpler three-state readout instead of complex mid-circuit checks. The core technical contribution is a specialized branch-and-bound decoder designed to handle the non-trivial constraints arising from leakage errors.
main_problem: The core problem is developing quantum error correction (QEC) circuits that achieve superior erasure error-correction capacity while minimizing hardware overhead associated with mid-circuit checks.
main_result: The authors show that the moonwalking surface code, when combined with three-state readout and assuming skip-gate leakage, can maintain erasure performance with zero overhead.
method: They introduce a specialized branch-and-bound decoder to solve the quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation (quasi-MLE) problem for decoding errors under strict disjointness constraints.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the surface code, comparing static, walking, and moonwalking variants. The system models error channels including leakage, Pauli errors, and erasures, analyzed using three-state readout.
key_observables: Logical error rate scaling under erasure conditions; syndrome extraction circuits (Z stabilizer measurements); minimum weight perfect matching solutions ($ ar{S}$).
important_parameters: The comparison is made across different leakage models (Depolarizing, Tailored, Skip-gate) and erasure check schedules.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include the faithfulness of three-state readout and modeling leaked qubits causing two-qubit gates to be entirely skipped (skip-gate model).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the gate sequences comparing walking vs. moonwalking circuits, showing how syndrome extraction is performed over multiple cycles. Other figures detail the structure of the branch-and-bound decoder algorithm flow.
paper_structure: The paper systematically studies error correction protocols, introducing the moonwalking code as an improvement. It then details the necessary decoding machinery—the branch-and-bound algorithm—to handle the complex constraints imposed by leakage and erasure information.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly detailed theoretical framework for fault-tolerant quantum computation, specifically addressing practical hardware limitations like mid-circuit measurement overheads in superconducting or trapped-ion architectures.
